chapters.title: Chapter 1: Article III Case-or-Controversy and Standing Fundamentals
chapters.description: Explains the constitutional limits on federal judicial power and the core elements of Article III standing that every federal case must satisfy.
subtopics: Case-or-controversy requirement and separation of powers rationale
Elements of standing: injury in fact, causation (traceability), and redressability
Concrete, particularized, actual or imminent injury
Burden of proof for standing at different litigation stages
Organizational standing and associational standing basics
Jurisdictional nature of standing and obligation to address it first

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Procedural-Injury and Informational-Injury Standing
chapters.description: Covers when a statutory procedure or informational right can support Article III standing and the limits on such theories.
subtopics: Distinguishing procedural from substantive rights for standing
Relaxed imminence and redressability in procedural-rights cases and their limits
Requirement of a concrete interest affected by the procedural violation
Informational standing: entitlement to specific information as a concrete injury
Differences between denial of access to records and denial of participation or notice
Examples from election law, sunshine laws, and FOIA contexts

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Causation and Redressability When Third Parties Control Outcomes
chapters.description: Analyzes standing’s traceability and redressability when relief depends on choices of nonparties or independent agencies.
subtopics: Independent third-party decisionmaking and speculative causal chains
Limits on relying on predictions about nonparty behavior
Distinction between judgments that bind parties versus opinions that may persuade nonparties
Impact of agency enforcement discretion on redressability
Strategic pleading pitfalls in multi-agency causal chains

chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Administrative Procedure Act—Reviewability and Agency Nonenforcement
chapters.description: Introduces APA doctrines governing when courts may review agency inaction or nonenforcement choices and when actions are committed to agency discretion.
subtopics: APA cause of action and 5 U.S.C. §§ 701–706 overview
§ 701(a)(2): Actions committed to agency discretion by law
Heckler v. Chaney presumption of unreviewability for nonenforcement
Exceptions to Chaney and recognizable legal standards
§ 706(1) claims to compel “discrete” action legally required (Norton v. SUWA)
Interaction between reviewability and Article III redressability

chapters.title: Chapter 5: APA Judicial Review—Final Agency Action, Standards, and Remedies
chapters.description: Details prerequisites and tools for reviewing federal agency action or inaction and the typical remedies courts provide.
subtopics: Final agency action under § 704
Record review and arbitrary-and-capricious standard under § 706(2)
Scope of § 706(1) relief to compel unlawfully withheld or unreasonably delayed action
Remand, vacatur, remand without vacatur, and declaratory/injunctive relief
Waiver of sovereign immunity under 5 U.S.C. § 702
Limits on directing specific enforcement outcomes

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Freedom of Information Act—Requests, Litigation, and Remedies
chapters.description: Provides the statutory framework for FOIA requests, agency obligations, judicial review, and remedies, including disciplinary-referral provisions.
subtopics: FOIA’s purpose, scope, and definitions of agency records
Request processing, searches (including email and electronic records), and exemptions
Administrative exhaustion and timelines
Judicial review: de novo review and remedies (injunction to produce, attorneys’ fees)
5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(F): Court-triggered referrals to OSC for potential discipline
Differences between FOIA’s disclosure remedy and personnel discipline mechanisms

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Civil Service Reform Act and the Office of Special Counsel
chapters.description: Explains the CSRA’s enforcement architecture, OSC’s investigatory and prosecutorial roles, and the MSPB’s adjudicatory functions.
subtopics: Overview of CSRA purposes and structure
OSC authority over prohibited personnel practices (5 U.S.C. § 1214)
Disciplinary actions and procedures (5 U.S.C. § 1215)
Other OSC investigative authority (5 U.S.C. § 1216), including FOIA-related misconduct
MSPB processes, corrective vs. disciplinary remedies, and standards
Notice and status-communication provisions in § 1214 and their applicability outside PPP cases

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Suing Federal Officials—Sovereign Immunity, Causes of Action, and Mandamus
chapters.description: Sets out pathways to challenge federal agency action or inaction and limits on compelling enforcement.
subtopics: Official-capacity suits and sovereign immunity
APA waiver of sovereign immunity and limits
Mandamus jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. § 1361) and standards for a clear, nondiscretionary duty
Ultra vires claims and their constraints
Overlap and distinctions among APA, mandamus, and specific statutory review schemes

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Federal Pleading and Motion Practice for Jurisdictional Issues
chapters.description: Covers how standing is tested and proven at the motion-to-dismiss stage and the applicable pleading standards.
subtopics: Rule 12(b)(1) vs. Rule 12(b)(6) in public law cases
Facial vs. factual jurisdictional challenges
Plausibility and factual allegations required to establish standing at the pleading stage
Use of affidavits and materials outside the pleadings for jurisdiction
Organizational plaintiffs: proving injury, causation, and redressability

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Appellate Jurisdiction, Standards of Review, and Remedies
chapters.description: Explains how appellate courts review dismissals, address standing sua sponte, and structure relief when jurisdiction is lacking.
subtopics: Final judgment rule and appealability of dismissals
De novo review of legal issues and standing determinations
Obligation to confirm subject-matter jurisdiction on appeal
Vacatur of merits judgments entered without jurisdiction
Remand with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Landmark Standing Precedents—Lujan, Summers, Akins, and Florida Audubon
chapters.description: Synthesizes central Supreme Court and D.C. Circuit cases shaping modern standing doctrine, especially for procedural and informational injuries.
subtopics: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife: injury in fact, causation, redressability; concrete and imminent harm
Summers v. Earth Island Institute: no standing for bare procedural rights without concrete harm
FEC v. Akins: informational injury when a statute entitles the plaintiff to information
Florida Audubon Society v. Bentsen (en banc): relaxed standards in procedural-rights cases and continuing need for concrete injury
Public Citizen v. DOJ and related informational-rights cases as doctrinal context

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Landmark Administrative and Redressability Precedents—Heckler v. Chaney and Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine
chapters.description: Explores core decisions limiting judicial review of agency nonenforcement and emphasizing redressability constraints involving third parties.
subtopics: Heckler v. Chaney: presumption against review of agency nonenforcement decisions
How enforcement discretion affects causation and redressability analyses
FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine: speculation about independent third parties cannot establish standing
Implications for suits seeking to compel investigations or enforcement
Related principles on judgments binding parties versus persuasive effects on nonparties
